Learned embeddings of navigable state spaces

Cognitive maps that know their own shape

A model learns to embed the states of a graph purely from which states are adjacent — no coordinates, no rewards, no action labels. The geometry it invents recovers true shortest paths, keeps entangled factors apart, and — the point of this log — organizes into strata of different dimension that match how many ways each state can move.

contrastive adjacency factored attention stratified geometry volume-growth dimension no state enumeration

01 — The idea

A map is a metric you can navigate

In neuroscience, a cognitive map is the brain's internal model of a space — the thing that lets you plan a route you've never walked. Here we build the toy version: a network embeds the nodes of a graph into a vector space so that distance in the embedding ≈ shortest-path distance in the graph. Do that well and the embedding is a map — you can read off how to get from any state to any goal.

The twist this project cares about is stratified spaces: spaces stitched together from pieces (strata) of different dimension. A point where two surfaces touch is higher-dimensional than the surfaces themselves; a state where an agent is frozen has fewer degrees of freedom than one where it can roam. Real state spaces are stratified, and a good map should reflect that — its local dimension should vary from place to place. This log shows that a plain contrastive embedding does exactly that, and that you can measure it.

02 — The state space

From two glued tori to agents with knobs

Two environments, same principle. The first is a pair of 15×15 wraparound tori joined at a single bridge node: to cross from one torus to the other you must pass through that one point, so the shortest path between the sheets always detours through it — a textbook stratified join.

The second scales the idea into varying dimension. Several agents live on a torus; each has a knob that restricts how it may move — all (2D), horizontal (1D), vertical (1D), or none (0D). A state's degrees of freedom is the sum over agents of their knob's dimension. Flip knobs and you move between strata of different dimension, from a frozen 0-D point up to a full 8-D torus with four free agents.

03 — Input

Two ways to hand a state to the model

The model never sees coordinates. A state arrives either as a small set of factored tokens — one per factor of variation (each agent's position, its knob, the torus id, a color) — or as a raw image, a grid of pixels the model must read.

In the image form, every pixel holds one of a few values: 0 background, 1 the agent, 2 a torus-identity marker, 3 a color marker. Identity and color live in two redundant marker pixels each, so that when the agent's pixel happens to sit on a marker, the other copy still shows it — the state stays fully observable under occlusion.

04 — Model

Attention builds the embedding; a norm makes it a metric

Query vectors cross-attend the input (the pixels, or the factor tokens) and a small transformer pools them into a single state embedding e(s). The learned distance between two states is then just a norm of the difference:

# self-norm distance head
D(u, v) = ‖ e(u) − e(v) ‖p

That norm turned out to be load-bearing. An earlier design read distance straight off a free scalar attention score, with no metric structure. It failed: with nothing enforcing a triangle inequality, training satisfied its pointwise constraints while the graded distances collapsed. Reading distance as a norm of an attention-built embedding restores identity and the triangle inequality — and the geodesic emerges. When actions matter, a small latent-dynamics network f(z, a) → z′ predicts the next state's embedding, so the effect of each action lives in the same space.

05 — Training

Only local truths; the global map emerges

The model is never told a shortest-path distance. It sees only local facts about the graph and has to invent the rest:

  • Neighbors sit one apart. States joined by an edge are pulled to distance ≈ 1.
  • Random pairs push apart. A repulsion term keeps the space from collapsing to a point (the trivial zero-loss solution).
  • Actions compose. When actions are used, latent dynamics is trained so f(za, action) lands on zb for each real transition.
  • Isometry (optional, sharpest). Instead of only 1-step edges, anchor pairs to their exact local geodesic. This flattens local patches so the geometry is faithful at every scale.

For the dimension experiments there are no actions at all — the model is trained purely on the adjacency structure, then we ask what geometry it built. Crucially, the training samples edges on the fly, so the state space is never enumerated: the four-agent space has on the order of 1011 states and is learned from sampled neighbors alone.

Why local-only matters The interesting claim isn't "a network can fit distances." It's that a metric-constrained embedding, shown nothing but which states touch, reconstructs the global geodesic — including forced detours and varying dimension — as an emergent property.

06 — Result · geometry

The detour becomes a shape

Trained on the bridged tori with local supervision only, the embedding recovers the true geodesic — and you can see the stratified join. Projected down, the metric space collapses onto a single dominant axis that is the distance to the bridge: the two tori appear as two arms meeting at the bridge node, and moving out along either arm is moving away from the crossing point. The forced detour is now literally a direction in space.

07 — Result · factors

Keeping the factors apart

A tempting hope is that a factored model separates its factors on its own — one part of the code for where the agent is, another for which world it's in. It does not, for free: left alone, both attention queries fixate on the agent and identity leaks in weakly. We ran a sweep of pressures to see what actually forces the split.

The clean winner is move-invariance: gently require one (unnamed) factor to stay constant as the agent moves — relative to its own spread, so it can't cheat by going dead. Because identity is exactly the thing that doesn't change when you walk around, that factor is forced to become identity, and it must read the static markers to do so. Independent factors (a color you can toggle anywhere) separate for free under sparsity; only coupled factors like position and identity need the nudge.

08 — Result · dimension

Reading the local dimension off the map

Now the headline. Train the embedding on the agents-and-knobs space (adjacency only) and it self-organizes into strata of different local dimension. To measure that dimension we borrow the Volume Growth Transform: around any point, count how many neighbors fall within a growing radius. On a d-dimensional manifold that count scales as rd, so the slope of log-count against log-radius is the local dimension.

count( ‖e − eq‖ < r ) ∝ rd → d = slope of log count vs log r

The key realization — and what makes this scale — is that dimension is local: you never need the whole state space, only enough neighbors around each query. So we sample each query's local ball on the fly (dedup the offsets — a 1-D stratum has only a handful of distinct points) and run the estimator there. No enumeration, any number of agents.

The embedding is genuinely stratified

Colored by degrees of freedom, the learned space visibly separates into pieces of different dimension, and the estimator's per-state reading rises monotonically with the true value. Frozen states collapse to a 0-dimensional point; a four-agent free state opens up to a full eight dimensions.

estimator (4 agents, DOF 0–8)correlationreads
ambient participation ratio0.96works, but over-counts curvature
volume-growth, coarse grid0.15fails — too few points to scale
volume-growth, dense local ball0.93intrinsic dimension recovered
+ multi-scale isometry training0.95near-identity ladder
TwoNN estimator0.53too sensitive on thin strata

Getting it to work took three things: a dense-enough local ball (a real scaling regime), deduping the ball (a 1-D stratum is only a few distinct points), and isometry training (flat local patches). The only stubborn residual is the very top — an 8-D ball is intrinsically under-sampled, the curse of dimensionality, and no grid removes it.

09 — In one breath

What the log adds up to

  • A map emerges from adjacency alone. Local "these two touch, cost 1" plus a metric prior reconstructs the global geodesic, detours included.
  • The metric prior is essential. Read distance as a norm of an attention-built embedding, not a free scalar — otherwise the graded structure collapses.
  • Coupled factors need an encoder-level nudge. Move-invariance splits position from identity; sparsity handles independent factors for free.
  • The map is stratified, and you can measure it. Local dimension varies with degrees of freedom and is read directly from the embedding by volume growth on a locally-sampled ball — no state-space enumeration, up to eight dimensions, correlation ≈ 0.95.
